change.title: AION Cambridge memory manufacture: 1975 establishment to Aurelia launch supply
change.reason: Accelerate the existing six-workstream programme with six major pre-launch milestones, a shared dated factory resource, separately qualified memory recipes and explicit Aurelia BOM sourcing. Preserve the established forecast +5% capacity policy, later stepper/ERAv1 dates and unresolved sales/first-offering facts. All changes form one atomic proposal because qualification events, process ownership, removed recruitment events and the supplied hardware must agree. Capacity calculations and a record-by-record audit are in data_storytelling/review_evidence/aion-memory-production/. Proposed acceptance narratives are alternative-history decisions for review, not fabricated laboratory evidence.

after.name: AION Labs Cambridge wafer fabrication and test facility
after.description: AION-operated 75 mm wafer fabrication, metrology, probe, final test and reliability facilities. External die assembly is a separately qualified supply route; the secret design facility is not a wafer factory.

statements: Adam established a secret engineering facility outside Logix Tech, AION Labs and AION Software.

He equipped it with a CAD workstation running Virtuoso, Spectre, Xcelium, Genus, Innovus, Tempus, Quantus and Pegasus, together with a HEIDELBERG DWL 66+ laser-lithography system brought from the 2020s.
The facility supplied advanced design work to the companies while concealing the origin of its tools.
Adam established a secret engineering facility outside Logix Tech, AION Labs and AION Software.

He equipped it with a CAD workstation running Virtuoso, Spectre, Xcelium, Genus, Innovus, Tempus, Quantus and Pegasus, together with a HEIDELBERG DWL 66+ laser-lithography system brought from the 2020s.
The facility supplied advanced design work to the companies while concealing the origin of its tools.

From February 1975, Adam can supply circuit designs, design-rule checks, test structures, mask data and master masks to accelerate memory development. Cambridge must verify mask tone, scale, overlay, defects and compatibility with its projection tools and qualify its own silicon.

The secret facility supplies no commercial wafer capacity, automatic licence rights or transferred production qualification. Contemporary process-transfer and second-source rights require separate agreements.

after.topic: Aurelia memory supply and protected Cambridge capacity, 1975–June 1978
statements: Fund the early fab, staffing, tools, working capital and qualification from Adam’s capital. Early ROM and SRAM sales provide customer feedback and operating revenue; they do not determine the pace of capital investment.

Plan for 10,000 Aurelias per month at the June 1978 launch, with an expansion scenario of 20,000. These are manufacturing planning cases, not recorded sales. Each computer consumes 32 16 Kbit DRAMs and two 4 Kbit SRAMs.

Use 30% attachment of the eight-chip 16 KiB RAM card as a provisioning scenario, without assigning its unresolved first commercial offering date. Reserve 100,000 accepted DRAMs and 10,000 accepted 4 Kbit SRAMs per month for external customers; these are planning allocations, not signed orders or guaranteed income.

Apply the existing finance premise once: forecast demand plus 5% good-output capacity. The 10,000-computer case therefore requires 466,200 DRAMs and 31,500 4 Kbit SRAMs per month. The 20,000-computer case requires 827,400 and 52,500 respectively. Do not add the earlier illustrative 10% allowance.

Before launch, fund and build one month of internal memory demand: 344,000 accepted DRAMs and 20,000 accepted 4 Kbit SRAMs, segregated from external orders. Replenish against consumption and revised demand; headroom does not imply permanent accumulation of unsold stock.

Provision 8,000 total wafer starts per month by December 1977: up to 6,000 DRAM, 500 4 Kbit SRAM, 500 ROM/1 Kbit SRAM, 500 released logic and 500 engineering starts. All allocations share one factory and its back-end capacity. Unused allocations may move only after route and load checks.

Require the March 1978 acceptance to demonstrate at least 575,000 accepted DRAMs and 31,500 accepted 4 Kbit SRAMs per month, or equivalent demonstrated spare capacity against actual shipments. Capacity demonstrations must cover the full route and shipped grade; forecasts are not measured results.

The 20,000-computer scenario requires expansion of DRAM, SRAM, assembly and test capacity. An option for up to 12,000 DRAM starts per month is an expansion objective, not installed capacity; no such capacity is credited to the initial line.

Recruit experienced process integration, DRAM, reliability, production test and maintenance staff early. Legitimate recruitment from established semiconductor manufacturers does not convey their trade secrets or process licences.

From May 1978, larger-memory and later processor research must stay inside the reserved engineering allocation or separately commissioned capacity; it must not consume committed Aurelia or external memory output.

before.name: AION wafer traceability, process control and yield engineering
before.description: Control of the Cambridge fabrication line through traceable lots, measured process windows, failure analysis and controlled recipe changes.

specification.description:
A wafer history connects material, equipment, recipe and electrical results. Process measurements and corrective action distinguish random defects from systematic drift.

Trace each wafer to material batch, tool, operator, recipe revision and electrical results; map defects and distinguish random from systematic failures.

Monitor particles, film thickness, sheet resistance, transistor thresholds, contacts and tool drift; use control charts and documented corrective action.

Engineering activity and released manufacture have different acceptance requirements. Yield reporting keeps wafer, die, package and saleable-output measures separate.

Separate engineering lots from released production; qualify maintenance and tool substitutions before customer manufacture.

Report wafer completion, electrical die yield, accepted speed/retention bins, package yield and good saleable chips per wafer separately.

after.name: AION wafer traceability, process control and yield engineering
after.description: Control of the Cambridge fabrication line through traceable lots, measured process windows, failure analysis and controlled recipe changes.

specification.description: Trace every wafer through incoming material, mask revision, tool, operator and recipe to its wafer map and final-test bin. Monitor particle adders, oxide thickness and integrity, sheet resistance, threshold voltage, junction leakage, contact resistance and alignment using control wafers and scribe-line structures. Separate random defects from systematic signatures; stop and contain affected lots when a control limit is exceeded.

Use split lots and designed experiments to isolate implant dose, oxidation, anneal, cleaning and contact effects. Release a change only after independent confirmation lots and reliability review. Qualify alternate tools and post-maintenance recovery with the same controls; retain golden wafers, spare critical assemblies and a frozen production route. Selected dry etches require layer-specific damage and residue qualification.

Report wafer completion as completed production wafers divided by started production wafers; accepted electrical yield as die meeting the released grade divided by gross candidate die on completed wafers; and assembly/final-test yield as accepted packaged parts divided by accepted die sent to assembly. Keep engineering wafers, rejects, downgraded bins and rework separately traceable. Good output per start is the product of gross die and these three fractions. Measure cycle-time distributions and work in process as well as output; do not confuse installed tools, forecasts or shipped volume with qualified spare capacity.

before.name: AION memory characterisation and production testing
before.description: Wafer-probe, packaged-device and reliability tests supporting separate ROM, SRAM and DRAM release decisions.

specification.description:
ROM, SRAM and DRAM need different electrical tests. Qualification spans the specified operating conditions and retains evidence that can be traced to lots and failures.

Qualify ROM image verification and SRAM read/write margins separately from DRAM retention, sensing, refresh and disturb behaviour.

Test across specified voltage and temperature limits; retain lot histories, wafer maps and failure-analysis evidence.

Redundancy can improve accepted output only on revisions that implement it. After supported repair, the complete device must be tested again; unrepaired launch designs receive no assumed repair benefit.

For repairable DRAM revisions, map defects, programme only supported redundancy and retest the complete device; unrepairable launch revisions receive no assumed repair benefit.

after.name: AION memory characterisation and production testing
after.description: Wafer-probe, packaged-device and reliability tests supporting separate ROM, SRAM and DRAM release decisions.

specification.description: Verify ROM images and address decoding against the customer-approved pattern; test SRAM reads, writes, standby current and pattern sensitivity. For DRAM, cover retention, refresh addressing, sense margins, coupling, disturb, leakage and supply sequencing. Run walking, checkerboard and March-style patterns with deliberately stressful addresses and transitions; correlate wafer and packaged tests against characterized samples. Define each timing grade at its specified voltage and temperature corners.

Qualify independent wafer lots and package lots, including alternate approved routes. Before release, specify sample sizes, acceptance limits and test conditions for powered high-temperature life, temperature cycling, humidity/package integrity and bond checks. A {life_hours}-hour powered life test uses multiple lots and documented junction temperature and electrical bias; it supports qualification, not an invented field failure rate. Contain failures, perform physical/electrical analysis and requalify the affected process or assembly change. Screening cannot substitute for correcting an unstable process.

Record probe maps, speed and retention bins, assembly traceability and final acceptance. Validate test coverage, calibration, fixture contact, test time and station availability against the committed mix; correlate independently staffed stations. Qualified outside assemblers receive controlled die maps and package drawings; AION owns incoming inspection and final release. Maintain an approved alternate assembly route and buffer stock against disruptions.

Map defects and programme redundancy only on revisions that physically implement it, followed by full retest. The initial 1 Kbit SRAM, 4 Kbit SRAM and 16 Kbit DRAM receive no assumed spare-row, laser-repair or future stepper yield benefit.

chapters.description: The factory processes {wafer_diameter_mm} mm wafers. Equipment groups below share material handling, utilities and staff; duplicate recipe records do not create extra machines. This configuration provisions capacity; dated acceptance events establish qualification.

Operate engineering and released customer lots under separate travellers. Match operator staffing, probe, assembly and final test to each accepted route before increasing releases; this configuration makes no Aurelia-volume throughput claim.

constraints.description: Supplier acceptance verifies uniformity, overlay, contamination and electrical results on the actual recipes. These equipment groups are procurement and qualification commitments; unspecified vendor model numbers or external supplier contracts are not represented as executed agreements.
Protect released customer lots from development experiments; qualify tools and trained shifts before transferring work.

For the mature 16 Kbit DRAM route, require wafer completion at least 90%, pooled accepted electrical die yield at least 60% across ten independent lots, no qualification lot below 50%, and assembly/final acceptance at least 95%. At the earlier DRAM release, 50% electrical die yield is the minimum. The 4 Kbit SRAM capacity case uses at least 50% electrical die yield and the same completion/assembly minima; ROM, 1 Kbit SRAM and logic retain their own grade-specific acceptance limits.

Measure throughput at the released grade over sustained production, including probe, package, screening and final test. Two stations at each test stage are initial installed minima, not proof of adequate throughput. Demonstrate hours at measured test times, and add stations before output acceptance if needed.

Qualify external package assembly with a second approved route; reserve at least the accepted-output requirement divided by 95% in die-loading capacity. Separate engineering and reliability samples from customer stock.

At the March 1978 gate, wafer cycle time has median at most 35 days and 90th percentile at most 45 days; assembly and final test take at most 14 additional days. Schedule lot cohorts and inventory by these delays.

The mature capacity calculation uses at least 190 candidate DRAM die per wafer and 160 candidate 4 Kbit SRAM die per wafer. Replace these planning values with the actual mask map and exclusions at acceptance; if output is insufficient, increase demonstrated capacity before claiming readiness.

Reserve the balance for SRAM, ROM, logic and setup; prove the complete mix and add stations before release if its measured loading exceeds availability. Qualification corner testing uses separately scheduled samples and does not silently consume production slots.

Check every thermal, implant, deposition, wet, metallisation and resist route using the actual wafer starts × recipe visits × cycle time, including batch fill, queueing and maintenance. Installed group counts do not establish throughput; any bottleneck must be expanded or its schedule reduced before the accepted-output gate. Raw-material stock is separate from finished-memory launch inventory.

before.title: Cambridge manufacturing team and pilot-line establishment
before.description: Recruit manufacturing leadership and establish a 75 mm silicon-gate NMOS pilot line with a 3 µm qualification objective. Use forgiving test structures during equipment bring-up.

inputs.description: AION Labs exists and can appoint staff and fund the Cambridge facility.

steps.description: Appoint the experienced manufacturing leadership and core integration team.
Purchase clean-area systems, ultrapure water, filtered gases, chemical handling and reliable temperature-controlled utilities.

Purchase and install Micralign projection lithography, resist coating/development, oxidation and diffusion furnaces, silicon/dielectric deposition, wet processing, metallisation, inspection and wafer probing.

Seek a licensed silicon-gate NMOS process-transfer package with training, design rules, test structures and reference wafers. Qualify the actual Cambridge route; a supplier or licence is not assumed from recruitment alone.
Hire equipment-maintenance, facilities, contamination-control and test technicians; contract supplier installation and training support.
Qualify 75 mm wafer handling and test structures; document process windows, tool acceptance and pilot electrical results.

outcomes.description: An accepted pilot line and documented process route support separate product qualification.

after.title: Cambridge manufacturing team and pilot-line establishment
after.description: Establish the Cambridge 75 mm silicon-gate NMOS pilot factory during 1975, using Adam’s design and mask advantage while qualifying every physical process locally.

inputs.description: The founding provides the organisation and capital mandate.

steps.description: January–March 1975: appoint a fab director, silicon-gate integration lead, lithography lead, facilities lead and test/reliability lead. Recruit experienced British, European and US semiconductor staff with relocation and long-term incentives; no named employer transfer or proprietary licence is presumed.
From February 1975, receive verified design rules, test structures and mask masters from the secret engineering facility; check projection-tool compatibility before exposing engineering wafers.

March–September 1975: procure clean areas, ultrapure water, filtered gases, chemical/exhaust systems and backup utilities. Order two compatible Micralign projection tools, two resist routes, segregated furnaces and wet benches, implant/anneal access, deposition, metallisation, metrology, probe and reliability equipment for the initial line configuration.

June–December 1975: train maintenance, facilities, contamination-control, test and shift technicians with supplier engineers; qualify critical spares and external failure-analysis and assembly support. Seek legitimate process-transfer training where useful, without assuming an executed licence. Qualify starting wafers and critical gas, chemical and package-material sources against released incoming specifications; establish alternate supply and replenishment lead times.

By December 1975: accept 75 mm handling, contamination controls, mask overlay, transistor/contact structures and electrical monitors. Establish engineering travellers and controlled recipes; installation does not itself release a commercial memory.
15 December 1975: accept the installed pilot route and its electrical control structures.

outcomes.description: The installed pilot factory and controlled 3 µm development route support separate product qualifications.

before.title: Commercial mask-ROM and small-SRAM qualification

inputs.description: The accepted pilot line can run product engineering lots.

steps.description: Hire ROM/SRAM product and applications engineers and a commercial lead for industrial controllers, instrumentation, terminals and peripherals.
Develop customer-specific mask ROM and a 1 Kbit SRAM; evaluate 4 Kbit SRAM only as a separate product qualification. Charge for ROM design/masks and seek minimum-order commitments.
Pursue licensed second-source contracts with explicit process-transfer, test, sales-right and customer-acceptance terms; no unexecuted licence or guaranteed customer demand is counted as income.
Install automated probing, memory testing, temperature fixtures and reliability ovens; initially qualify external assembly suppliers and retain AION final-test responsibility.
Qualify independent wafer lots and customer-approved ROM images, packages, timing and SRAM margins.

outcomes.description: Released mask-ROM and initial SRAM recipes provide commercial manufacturing experience and product-specific test methods.

inputs.description: The accepted pilot line can run product engineering lots.

By June 1976: qualify external die assembly and its alternate route, retain AION final release, correlate independent probe/final-test stations and validate reliability fixtures.

before.title: 16 Kbit DRAM development and production qualification

inputs.description: The pilot fab provides the platform for DRAM-specific process development.

steps.description: Recruit DRAM device, sensing and memory-test specialists.
Purchase ion implantation and annealing capability, and qualify the deposition/patterning sequence required by the selected capacitor structure.
Use small arrays or a 4 Kbit engineering vehicle to isolate leakage, sensing and refresh faults; an intermediate commercial release is not required.
Develop the 16 Kbit array and sensing circuits; qualify retention, disturb behaviour, supply sequencing, package and timing.
Extend temperature-controlled wafer and packaged testing, reliability screening and failure analysis; prove repeatability across independent lots.

outcomes.description: The 16 Kbit DRAM recipe and memory-test methods support Aurelia supply.

after.title: 16 Kbit DRAM development and production qualification

inputs.description: The company provides funding and recruitment authority.

steps.description: June 1975: recruit a DRAM integration lead, capacitor/device engineer, sense-amplifier designer and memory-test lead. Offer relocation, equipment budgets and long-term incentives; recruitment conveys neither proprietary process rights nor an already qualified route.

July–December 1975: choose the storage-cell/capacitor route and test structures; procure and qualify implant, annealing and film-patterning support with the fab team. Review oxide integrity, leakage, substrate bias and sensing margins before committing the full array.
December 1975: use the accepted pilot route for DRAM engineering wafers.
January–September 1976: use small arrays and a 4 Kbit engineering vehicle to isolate retention, refresh, disturb and pattern sensitivity. This vehicle is not a separate commercial offering.

October 1976–June 1977: iterate the 16K×1 array, 128-row refresh and 4116-compatible power/timing contract. Use Adam’s checked masks to shorten design iterations, without bypassing silicon characterization.

July–September 1977: qualify at least three independent lots and the complete grade-specific electrical drawing, including voltage/temperature corners, package reliability and the 1,000-hour multi-lot life-test plan.

inputs.description: Recurring qualified product lots provide failure maps and operational evidence for yield improvement.

steps.description: Appoint the permanent yield, failure-analysis and maintenance group.
Purchase film-thickness, sheet-resistance and transistor measurement equipment, improved inspection, and scanning-electron-microscope access; link wafer maps to lot histories.
Improve cleaning, filtration, gas purity, contamination monitoring and preventive maintenance; stock spares and duplicate bottleneck tools where justified.
Qualify plasma stripping and selected dry-etch operations layer by layer, controlling damage, residues and dimensions.
Run controlled experiments on implants, oxidation, annealing and contacts. Release improvements only after independent production lots pass electrical and reliability limits.
Measure wafer completion, electrical yield, accepted bins, package yield, good chips per wafer and recurring cost separately; do not count forecast yields as observed results.

outcomes.description: Repeatable 3 µm logic manufacture and controlled ROM/SRAM/DRAM routes support subsequent product ramps.

inputs.description: The company funds a permanent factory-control and maintenance team.

steps.description: September 1975: appoint a yield manager, failure-analysis engineer, process-control engineers and maintenance specialists with authority to hold suspect lots and reject uncontrolled recipe changes. Procure metrology and contracted SEM access; retain wafer maps and lot histories from the first engineering runs.

October 1975–September 1976: control particles, film thickness, thresholds, leakage and contacts; correlate defects with tools and process windows. Establish spare assemblies, preventive maintenance and recovery qualification. Learn from initial ROM/SRAM lots without mixing forecast and observed yields.

January 1977: commission a third compatible projection tool and qualify alternate routes. Use controlled experiments for implants, oxidation, annealing and contacts; qualify plasma stripping and selected dry etches layer by layer.

By December 1977: commission a fourth projection tool, train full shift coverage and demonstrate the 8,000-start mixed-factory schedule. Reserve 6,000 starts for DRAM and four 500-start allocations for 4 Kbit SRAM, ROM/1 Kbit SRAM, logic and engineering. Match assembly bookings, probe and final-test station hours to the actual mix. Qualify two starting-wafer supply routes and fund a 16,000-wafer incoming-material buffer for the shared schedule.

January–March 1978: measure ten independent production lots across weeks and approved routes. Verify actual gross die, grade yields, reliability, cycle-time distributions, good output, tester hours and one-aligner-down memory protection. A projected wafer calculation alone cannot pass the acceptance. From February, reserve accepted released-product lots for the quarter-funded launch build; do not wait until the March capacity gate to start every inventory wafer.
31 March 1978: accept sustained memory output and controlled 3 µm production.

April–May 1978: complete funded launch inventory from previously started, released-product cohorts, qualify mainboard/video/card refresh and power sequencing with released parts, and reconcile reserved stock against external orders. Keep the RAM card’s first public offering date unresolved until separately established.
15 May 1978: accept Aurelia memory integration and launch supply.

outcomes.description: Factory control and memory-test methods support separately accepted shared-line capacity and qualified recipe output.
Mainboard RAM, built-in video memory and the optional RAM-card design are qualified against the released AION memory interfaces.

after.title: Cambridge sustained memory output accepted
after.description: The four-tool factory demonstrates the released memory mix across ten independent production lots spanning weeks and qualified routes. DRAM wafer completion is at least 90%, pooled accepted electrical die yield at least 60% with no qualification lot below 50%, and assembly/final acceptance at least 95%. Sustained accepted output or verified equivalent spare capacity reaches 575,000 DRAMs and 31,500 4 Kbit SRAMs per month. Actual wafer maps, tester hours and assembly throughput support the result; estimates alone cannot establish it. Median wafer cycle is at most 35 days, its 90th percentile at most 45 days, followed by at most 14 days for assembly/final test. One projection-tool outage preserves the memory schedule by pausing engineering and some logic starts. Released ROM/SRAM/DRAM and independent logic vehicles demonstrate control; future 64 Kbit DRAM and ERAv1 remain separately qualified.

The stock covers one month of the 10,000-computer planning case plus the 30% RAM-card provision. Sustained replenishment, assembly capacity and external allocations are reconfirmed before June launch. This is memory-subsystem readiness, not proof that every custom IC or the complete computer has passed production release.

chapters.description:
The card adds {capacity_kb} KiB to {host_base_computer_aurelia}, raising lower RAM from 44 to 60 KiB before workspace reservations. Eight {dram_id} chips form an 8-bit bank. Its four 4 KiB pages occupy B000–EFFF in the normal mapping; the existing common system RAM remains at F000–FFFF.

The card occupies one expansion slot. Install it with power off and restart: firmware discovers, tests and maps the pages without address switches. Common-memory service routines save the mapping, temporarily select ROM or video RAM and restore the card pages on return. The host schedules refresh independently of CPU mapping and refreshes all 128 rows within 2 ms even while the card is overlaid. The card decoder forwards those refresh cycles while suppressing ordinary accesses when deselected; board acceptance tests this interface and the three-rail power sequencing with the released AION part.
